description: Develops tropical cyclone heat-engine dynamics and uses Hurricane Harvey (2017) to distinguish wind category, storm surge, rainfall flooding, track uncertainty, and event attribution.

related_resources.reason: Warm-ocean depth, moisture, shear, latitude and disturbance requirements for genesis.
Eye and eyewall, spiral convection, changes in storm structure.
Large-scale steering and eyewall replacement over storm life cycles.
Maximum sustained wind only; excludes rain, surge, flooding and tornado hazards.
Rainfall flooding, surge versus storm tide, winds, tornadoes and surf.
Observed 2017 storm course and extreme rainfall including >60 inches at some Texas stations.
Inundation, streamflow, physical impact of extreme rainfall and watershed modeling.
Assesses heavy precipitation, drought, heat, convective storms, cyclones, and conditional event attribution.

background: Introduces rotation, ocean-atmosphere energy exchange, and flooding from everyday concepts; Hurricane Harvey is a case rather than a prerequisite.
readiness_checks: Why does a warm sea not guarantee tropical cyclogenesis?
Why can maximum wind decrease during increasing flood danger?
Why is the Saffir-Simpson category insufficient for evaluating surge?
How is a storm-track forecast different from a rainfall forecast?
What is attributed when researchers find human influence on hurricane rainfall?

period.label: Hurricane Harvey (2017) case study
period.note: Describes the historical case used to teach timeless cyclone mechanisms; not a date of scientific discovery.
